newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-RBA, U.S. poll focus for Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-RBA, U.S. poll focus for Australia.

text.p: Australian financial markets look set for a choppy week of trading with speculation of a local rate cut seen dominating trading tactics.
The board of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) meets on Tuesday and economists are divided over whether the RBA will move to ease monetary policy as early as Wednesday.
Analysts forecasts focus on a cut of 0.5 percentage points, which would lower the official cash rate to 6.5 percent.
The RBA last cut the official cash rate by 0.5 percentage points to 7.00 percent on July 31 this year.

The main economic release this week is October employment data due out Thursday. The Reuters survey of economists forecasts a median rise of 13,000 for October employment following a steeper than expected fall in September but not by enough to bring the unemployment rate down from 8.7 percent.

U.S. Treasuries ended lower in New York on Friday after profit-taking ahead of the U.S. election on Tuesday and a quarterly Treasury refunding next week wiped out an early advance. The early gain was scored after the government reported only moderate October U.S. payroll growth of 210,000 jobs. The unemployment rate remained steady at 5.2 percent.
U.S. blue-chip stocks closed lower as the market reflected the nervousness of bond traders ahead of Tuesday's elections.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10-yr cash yield 6.59, 3-yr 6.67)

Australian bonds face a volatile trading week, which it should start with a weaker tone following the fall in U.S. Treasuries. Local traders will note the caution of U.S. traders ahead of the U.S. election which wiped out gains made by Treasuries after a moderate October U.S. payroll growth report. The key event locally will likely be on Wednesday, the day after the Reserve Bank board meeting, when there is a strong possibility that an easing in policy will be announced given recent data showing that the economy is in need of stimulus.
The market is already pricing in a 50 basis points easing, so there is a lot of room for disappointment, particularly at the short-end if official rates are kept at 7.0 percent.

"Significant data releases are fairly thin on the ground in the U.S. next week. Elections and auctions will occupy the market's attention," Commonwealth Bank economists said in their weekly economic update.
The release of October employment data on Thursday is likely to provide the debt markets with some interest following September's steeper than expected employment fall of 34,100.
The U.S. market is also likely to provided strong leads over the course of the week with the U.S. election on Tuesday and three legged quarterly refunding auctions starting the same day.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7896/01, NY US$7889/94)
The Australian dollar may this week finally get to escape the suffocating US$0.7850/7985 range that has held it for almost two months.

"The AUD will walk a tightrope in the coming week. Commodity prices have dropped sharply. The main support is overseas investors chasing yield. However a rate cut is on the cards," the Colonial State Bank said in its weekly market update.

The chance of a break rests with the RBA's decision on interest rates at its board meeting Tuesday, although it was far from clear cut how the market would actually react to the different permutations.
Dealers reckoned a 0.5 point rate cut was priced in and, after an initial wobble, the dollar could well rally once it was out of the way.
However, that sanguine view rested on the vital assumption the easing would not be more than 0.5 point and would be the last in the cycle.

That was not so certain following a run of weak economic data recently and if the RBA was seen to have left open the option of another move down the track, offshore investors were likely to react much more bearishly.
In such a case, dealers thought the dollar could well test the September low of US$0.7850 with a risk of a break down to US$0.7810.

On the other hand, if the RBA did not move by Wednesday -- this was seen as the make or break day -- the market would assume a cut was off the agenda until late November or early December and a lot of short covering would ensue.
That could see the currency re-test US$0.7985, although a dealers doubted levels above 80 cents could be sustained with the threat of an easing still lurking ahead.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ordinaries 2,339.4, down 10.8)

Australian shares are seen starting the week cautiously on with market action likely to be dominated by continued speculation of a local rate-cut, especially after the Reserve Bank of Australia's board meeting on Tuesday.

"The outlook is mostly positive, especially if base metal prices continue to firm. The risk lies with any major weakness on Wall Street or if the Reserve Bank doesn't move on rates," a dealer at a Sydney-based brokerage said.
Wall Street stocks ended lower on Friday as investors stepped to the sidelines ahead of the U.S. elections on Tuesday.

Analysts said although President Bill Clinton's re-election was widely anticipated by the market, Wall Street's worry had shifted to the possibility of a Democratic sweep of the Congressional races that may bring more tax and spending.

Base metal prices as always are a key focal point for investors in Australian equities. Major resource groups BHP and MIM are likely to find early support after copper continued its rise on the London Metal Exchange on Friday.

Local market interest will also be tuned into big firms holding their annual meetings this week; these include GIO Australia Ltd in Sydney on Monday, TNT Ltd and John Fairfax Holdings Ltd in Sydney on Wednesday, Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd in Sydney on Thursday and Brambles Ltd in Melbourne on Friday. News Corp Ltd is also expected to release first quarter results this week.
